## What it catches

A shell history file deleted, shredded, truncated or linked to the null device, or a shell started to run the history clearing command. The history file is the first record of what an intruder typed, so removing it hides the session. Clearing typed inside an interactive shell is a shell built-in and starts no process.

```yaml
selection_file:
  Image|endswith:
  - /rm
  - /shred
  - /truncate
  CommandLine|contains:
  - .bash_history
  - .zsh_history
selection_link:
  Image|endswith: /ln
  CommandLine|contains|all:
  - /dev/null
  - _history
selection_builtin:
  CommandLine|re: (?i)history\s+-c(\s|;|&|"|$)
condition: 1 of selection_*
```

## Tested on

- fires: `bash history deleted`
- fires: `root's bash history shredded`
- fires: `zsh history truncated to nothing`
- fires: `bash history linked to the null device`
- fires: `history cleared by a one-line shell`
- fires: `zsh history deleted`
- quiet: `reading the history file`
- quiet: `deleting a build log`
- quiet: `linking a release folder`
- quiet: `silencing a debug log through the null device`
- quiet: `showing the last commands`
- quiet: `counting a word in the history file`
- quiet: `listing the null device and the history file`
- quiet: `a link to the history file made by a backup script`

## False positives

- Provisioning and image templating scripts that empty the history before a machine image is taken
- Users who clear their own history out of habit

## What it does not see

- The clearing command typed in an interactive shell, a built-in that starts no process
- History never written because the shell was started with the history file unset
- History files of other shells and tools than bash and zsh

## First checks

- Identify the session: the user, the parent process and the source address of the logon
- Read the other commands of the same session in the process creation log
- Check authentication logs for the minutes before the history was cleared
